content: In Tanzania and Zambia, a study randomized 1,999 adults living with HIV who had not previously received antiretroviral therapy (ART) and had CD4 counts below 200 cells/mm³. Participants were assigned to either standard care or an enhanced care package. The enhanced care included serum cryptococcal antigen screening, pre-emptive antifungal treatment for those testing positive, and additional community support. This support involved weekly home or community visits by trained lay workers who delivered ART, provided adherence support, and monitored for drug toxicity or new symptoms. The intervention group experienced a 28% reduction in mortality, with a death rate of 13% compared to 18% in the standard care group. The REALITY trial enrolled 1,805 participants, mostly adults with HIV (72 were aged 5–17 years), with CD4 counts below 100 cells/mm³ in Kenya, Malawi, Uganda, and Zimbabwe. All participants were screened for active tuberculosis (TB) at enrollment and randomized to either standard care (co-trimoxazole) or an enhanced prophylaxis package. The enhanced package included 12 weeks of fluconazole, a fixed-dose combination of co-trimoxazole, isoniazid, and pyridoxine, a five-day course of azithromycin, and a single dose of albendazole. All drugs were initiated simultaneously, and ART was started on the same day. Over 24 weeks, the enhanced prophylaxis group showed a 28% reduction in TB incidence, a 62% reduction in cryptococcal disease, and a 17% reduction in hospitalizations compared to the standard care group. Most deaths occurred within the first three weeks, emphasizing the importance of early prophylaxis in advanced HIV disease. Implementing a package of essential interventions for advanced HIV disease focuses on preventing, diagnosing, and treating the most common causes of morbidity and mortality. Identifying individuals with advanced HIV disease requires CD4 testing. Additionally, determining immune status in those with virological treatment failure can guide clinical decisions. Attention should also be given to other severe illnesses not covered by the package, particularly in regions with prevalent comorbidities. Increased pill burden and side effects may affect adherence, so shorter TB preventive regimens are recommended. Research is needed to identify suitable screening tools. Cryptococcal disease is a significant opportunistic infection in advanced HIV disease and a major contributor to mortality. Early diagnosis and treatment of cryptococcal meningitis are critical to reducing mortality. Health professionals should maintain a low threshold for suspecting cryptococcal meningitis in advanced HIV cases. Countries should prioritize access to rapid cryptococcal antigen assays, preferably lateral flow assays, for use in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), serum, plasma, or whole blood. Immediate ART initiation is not recommended for individuals with cryptococcal meningitis due to the risk of increased mortality; ART should be deferred for 4–6 weeks after starting antifungal treatment. In resource-limited settings, India ink staining may be used, though it has lower sensitivity. If lumbar puncture is contraindicated, rapid serum or plasma cryptococcal antigen assays are recommended. Screening for cryptococcal antigen followed by pre-emptive antifungal therapy is advised for individuals with CD4 counts below 100 cells/mm³ to prevent invasive disease. Fluconazole prophylaxis is recommended when antigen screening is unavailable. Treatment of cryptococcal meningitis includes a preferred induction regimen of amphotericin B and flucytosine for two weeks, followed by fluconazole for consolidation and maintenance phases. Routine use of corticosteroids during induction is not recommended. ART initiation should be delayed for 4–6 weeks in cases of cryptococcal meningitis to avoid immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), which can occur in 10–50% of cases and is associated with high mortality. Histoplasmosis, caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, is another opportunistic infection in advanced HIV disease, particularly in endemic regions. Disseminated histoplasmosis presents with nonspecific symptoms, often resembling TB, complicating diagnosis. Diagnosis involves detecting circulating histoplasma antigens. Treatment for severe cases includes amphotericin B for two weeks, while mild-to-moderate cases are treated with itraconazole. Maintenance therapy with itraconazole for 12 months is recommended, though shorter durations may be considered if the patient is clinically stable, on ART, and has improved immune status. Children under five years old living with HIV are considered to have advanced disease due to high rates of severe immunosuppression. Advanced HIV disease in children is defined as WHO stage 3 or 4 or a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³ for those aged five years or older. Major causes of morbidity and mortality in children with HIV include pneumonia, TB, bloodstream infections, diarrheal disease, and severe malnutrition. Routine interventions such as deworming, malaria prophylaxis, and nutritional supplementation should be provided. Screening and prevention components for children include systematic TB screening, rapid diagnostic tests, and prophylaxis for opportunistic infections.
